text: The LORD said to Moses and Aaron,

"When someone has a swelling, a rash, or a bright spot on the skin of the body, and it develops into a case of a defiling skin disease, he must be brought to Aaron the priest or to one of his sons, the priests.

The priest shall examine the sore on the skin. If the hair in the sore has turned white and the sore appears to be deeper than the surrounding skin, it is a defiling skin disease. When the priest has examined him, he shall declare him unclean.
But if the bright spot on the skin is white and does not appear deeper than the skin, and the hair in it has not turned white, the priest shall isolate the affected person for seven days.
On the seventh day the priest shall examine him, and if the sore looks unchanged and has not spread in the skin, the priest shall isolate him for another seven days.

On the seventh day the priest shall examine him again, and if the sore has faded and has not spread in the skin, the priest shall declare him clean; it is only a rash. He shall wash his clothes, and he will be clean.
But if the rash does spread in the skin after he has shown himself to the priest and been declared clean, he must appear before the priest again.
The priest shall examine him, and if the rash has spread in the skin, the priest shall declare him unclean; it is a defiling disease.
When anyone has a case of defiling skin disease, he must be brought to the priest.
The priest shall examine him, and if there is a white swelling in the skin that has turned the hair white, and there is raw flesh in the swelling,
it is a chronic skin disease, and the priest shall declare him unclean. He is not to isolate him, for he is already unclean.
If the disease breaks out all over the skin and, as far as the priest can see, covers the person's skin from head to foot,
then the priest shall examine him, and if the disease has covered his whole body, he shall declare the affected person clean. Since it has all turned white, he is clean.
But whenever raw flesh appears on him, he will be unclean.
When the priest sees the raw flesh, he shall declare him unclean. The raw flesh is unclean; it is a defiling disease.
If the raw flesh changes and turns white, he must go to the priest.
The priest shall examine him, and if the sore has turned white, the priest shall declare the affected person clean; then he is clean.
When someone has a boil on his skin and it heals,
and in the place of the boil a white swelling or a reddish-white spot appears, he must show himself to the priest.

The priest shall examine it, and if it appears lower than the surrounding skin and the hair in it has turned white, the priest shall declare him unclean. It is a defiling disease that has broken out where the boil was.

versions.text: The priest shall examine it, and if it appears to be beneath the skin and the hair in it has turned white, the priest shall declare him unclean. It is a defiling disease that has broken out where the boil was.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew שָׁפָל מִן־הָעוֹר means the spot looks depressed or lower than the surrounding skin surface, not that it lies under the skin. "Beneath the skin" could mislead a listener into thinking the sore is subcutaneous; it also mirrors the wording of the parallel phrase in vv. 3 and 25 ("deeper than the skin").

text: But if the priest examines it and there is no white hair in it, and it is not lower than the surrounding skin but has faded, the priest shall isolate him for seven days.

versions.text: But if the priest examines it and there is no white hair in it, and it is not beneath the skin but has faded, the priest shall isolate him for seven days.
versions.explanation: Same issue as verse 20: the Hebrew describes the spot as not being depressed below the level of the skin, rather than not being under the skin. Consistency across vv. 20, 21, 26 also helps the oral reader.

text: But if it does spread further in the skin, the priest shall declare him unclean; it is an infection.

versions.text: If it spreads in the skin, the priest shall declare him unclean; it is a defiling disease.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew here reads simply נֶגַע הִוא, "it is an infection/sore," without the word צָרַעַת. The verse deliberately stops short of naming it a defiling skin disease (contrast v. 25, which does say נֶגַע צָרַעַת). Adding "defiling disease" imports content not in the text.

versions.text: If it spreads in the skin, the priest shall declare him unclean; it is an infection.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew opens with the connective וְאִם ("but if"), marking the contrast with the alternative outcome in v. 23, and uses the emphatic infinitive absolute פָּשֹׂה תִפְשֶׂה ("indeed spreads / spreads further") after the seven-day isolation. Rendering both the connective and the emphasis makes the two-branch structure clearer for a listener.

text: But if the spot stays where it is and does not spread, it is only the scar from the boil, and the priest shall declare him clean.
When someone has a burn on his skin and a reddish-white or white spot appears in the raw flesh of the burn,

the priest shall examine it. If the hair in the spot has turned white and it appears to be deeper than the skin, it is a defiling disease that has broken out in the burn. The priest shall declare him unclean; it is a defiling skin disease.
But if the priest examines it and there is no white hair in the spot, and it is not lower than the surrounding skin but has faded, the priest shall isolate him for seven days.

versions.text: But if the priest examines it and there is no white hair in the spot, and it is not beneath the skin but has faded, the priest shall isolate him for seven days.
versions.explanation: As in vv. 20-21, שְׁפָלָה refers to the spot appearing lower than the surface of the skin, not lying beneath it.

text: On the seventh day the priest shall examine him, and if it has spread in the skin, the priest shall declare him unclean; it is a defiling skin disease.
But if the spot stays where it is, has not spread in the skin, and has faded, it is only a swelling from the burn, and the priest shall declare him clean, for it is only the scar of the burn.
When a man or a woman has a sore on the head or the chin,

the priest shall examine the sore. If it appears to be deeper than the skin and the hair in it is yellow and thin, the priest shall declare that person unclean. It is a scaly infection, a defiling disease of the head or the chin.
But if the priest examines the infection and it does not appear to be deeper than the skin, and there is no black hair in it, the priest shall isolate the affected person for seven days.
On the seventh day the priest shall examine the sore, and if the infection has not spread, there is no yellow hair in it, and it does not appear to be deeper than the skin,
the person shall shave himself, but not the infected area, and the priest shall isolate him for another seven days.

On the seventh day the priest shall examine the infection, and if it has not spread in the skin and does not appear to be deeper than the skin, the priest shall declare him clean. He shall wash his clothes, and he will be clean.
But if the infection does spread in the skin after he has been declared clean,
the priest shall examine him, and if the infection has spread in the skin, he need not look for yellow hair; the person is unclean.
But if in his judgment the infection is unchanged and black hair has grown in it, the infection has healed. He is clean, and the priest shall declare him clean.
When a man or a woman has spots on the skin, white spots,
the priest shall examine them. If the spots on the skin are a dull white, it is only a harmless rash that has broken out on the skin; that person is clean.
If a man loses the hair from his head, he is bald, but he is clean.
If he loses the hair from the front of his head, he has a bald forehead, but he is clean.
But if there is a reddish-white sore on the bald head or the bald forehead, it is a defiling disease breaking out on his bald head or bald forehead.

versions.text: But if there is a reddish-white sore on the bald head or the bald forehead, it is a defiling disease breaking out on his head or forehead.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew repeats בְּקָרַחְתּוֹ אוֹ בְגַבַּחְתּוֹ ("on his bald head or his bald forehead"). Dropping "bald" in the second clause loses the deliberate repetition that ties the verdict to the bald areas just defined in vv. 40-41.

text: The priest shall examine him, and if the swollen sore on his bald head or forehead is reddish-white, like a defiling skin disease,
the man is diseased and unclean. The priest must declare him unclean; the sore is on his head.
Anyone with such a defiling disease must wear torn clothes, let his hair hang loose, cover the lower part of his face, and call out, "Unclean! Unclean!"
As long as he has the disease he remains unclean. He must live alone; his dwelling shall be outside the camp.
When a garment is contaminated with mildew—any woolen or linen garment,
any woven or knitted material of linen or wool, any leather, or anything made of leather—
and the contamination is greenish or reddish—in the garment, the leather, the woven or knitted material, or any leather article—it is a defiling mildew and must be shown to the priest.

versions.text: and the contamination in the garment, the leather, the woven or knitted material, or any leather article is greenish or reddish, it is a spreading mildew and must be shown to the priest.
versions.explanation: "Spreading" is not in the Hebrew here; spreading (פָּשָׂה) is only determined later, at the seventh-day inspection (v. 51). Calling it "spreading" at this stage pre-judges the diagnosis.

versions.text: and the contamination in the garment, the leather, the woven or knitted material, or any leather article is greenish or reddish, it is a defiling mildew and must be shown to the priest.
versions.explanation: In the Hebrew the color words follow immediately after "the contamination," and the list of materials comes afterward. The current word order forces the listener to hold a five-item list in mind before reaching the predicate; placing the color first and the list in an aside follows the Hebrew order and reads more easily aloud.

text: The priest shall examine it and shall isolate the affected article for seven days.

On the seventh day he shall examine it, and if the contamination has spread in the garment, in the woven or knitted material, or in the leather, whatever its use, it is a destructive mildew; the article is unclean.
He must burn the garment, or the woven or knitted material of wool or linen, or any leather article that is contaminated, because it is a destructive mildew; it must be burned in the fire.

versions.text: He must burn the garment, or the woven or knitted material of wool or linen, or any leather article that is contaminated, because it is a destructive mildew; it must be burned up.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew specifies "in the fire" (בָּאֵשׁ), an emphatic repetition after "he must burn." "Burned up" also reads flatly; "burned in the fire" preserves the force and reads well aloud.

text: But if the priest examines it and the contamination has not spread in the garment, in the woven or knitted material, or in the leather article,
he shall order that the contaminated article be washed, and he shall isolate it for another seven days.

After the article has been washed, the priest shall examine it, and if the spot has not changed its appearance, then even though it has not spread, it is unclean. You must burn it in the fire; it is a rotting spot, whether on the inside or the outside.

versions.text: After the article has been washed, the priest shall examine it, and if the spot has not changed its appearance, then even though it has not spread, it is unclean. Burn it, whether the rot is on the back or the front.
versions.explanation: "In the fire" (בָּאֵשׁ) is omitted, and the bare imperative "Burn it" shifts abruptly from the surrounding third-person instructions. For fabric and leather, קָרַחַת/גַבַּחַת are better rendered "inside or outside" rather than "back or front," which sounds like a description of a head.

text: But if the priest examines it and the spot has faded after the washing, he shall tear that part out of the garment, the leather, or the woven or knitted material.
If it appears again in the garment, in the woven or knitted material, or in any leather article, it is spreading, and whatever is contaminated must be burned.
Any garment, woven or knitted material, or leather article that has been washed and from which the contamination has disappeared, must be washed a second time, and it will be clean.
These are the instructions concerning contamination by mildew in woolen or linen garments, in woven or knitted material, or in any leather article, for pronouncing them clean or unclean.
